rationale: A wins because it keeps the story where the facts are and marks the weak planks before anyone steps on them. Its “Can a 1.8B model really match one 4x its size?” angle is a real verification story; B’s “A Fortune 100 manufacturer just became an early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model” splices two facts into a claim the update does not make. B has usable bones, but it gets seduced by market-structure drama before it has the proof.
gaps_in_A: “a credibility signal for open-source AI inside a regulated, conservative buyer” overreads the manufacturer fact; the update says Fortune 100 manufacturer, not regulated buyer or conservative buyer.
“A Fortune 100 manufacturer is an early customer of Hugging Face's paid enterprise hub” is valid but should sit below the pitch line until the actual name, use case, and on-record permission exist.
“Next step: journalist-fit-check” is a little premature for the benchmark and customer angles; reproduction evidence and customer clearance come before matching reporters.
gaps_in_B: “early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model” is invented. The update says early enterprise hub customer, not customer for the offline model.
“every major AI lab depends on” is a sweeping market-structure claim not supplied by the update. That is how a pitch walks itself into a fact-checking wall.
“data-residency and audit requirements” and “security-conscious buyers” may be plausible, but the update gives no regulated sector, compliance use case, or buyer quote. Plausible is not sourced.
“which is exactly the point for security-conscious buyers” treats an inferred positioning message as fact. The set asks for proof later, but the headline already spent the money.
